notes:
Slice 'surveillance' (2013–2022, with a few later outcomes of the same cases through 2025): the Snowden disclosures; rights restated in courts and statutes (Google Spain, Schrems I/II, GDPR, Puttaswamy, Carpenter, CCPA/CPRA, LGPD, PIPL, Colorado); the consent-banner era (GDPR application, Planet49, IAB Europe's TCF, Apple's ATT prompt, Google's abandoned cookie plan); scandals and penalties (Equifax, Cambridge Analytica, FTC v Facebook, Clearview AI, Kochava, Meta €1.2bn); and the first person-side signals given legal force (CCPA global-privacy-control rule, Global Privacy Control, Sephora, Colorado's universal opt-out). A 'signals' array profiles the era's four mechanisms (IAB TCF, GPC, ATT, Colorado UOOM) for comparison with IEEE 7012 / MyTerms.

Method: every CONFIRMED quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and re-checked with --check (all FOUND at last run). EU texts: eur-lex.europa.eu and curia.europa.eu's judgment viewer block scripted access, so the identical Official Journal and ECR texts were read from the EU Publications Office's Cellar repository (publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/...; CELEX numbers given in notes); CJEU press releases were read on curia.europa.eu. Some sites refused the helper's user agent (w3.org) — for those, the page was downloaded with curl into the helper's cache and then checked; Brazil's Planalto page is Windows-1252 and was transcoded to UTF-8 before checking. The California leginfo site timed out and was read via the Internet Archive. Non-English quotes (Italian, Portuguese, Chinese) are given in the original with translations in notes.

Could not verify / caveats: (1) California Secretary of State vote counts for Proposition 24 (9,384,625 yes, 56.2%) were read from the Statement of Vote table but the PDF text layer scrambles cells, so that source is PENDING. (2) The Guardian's Verizon story is dated 5 June 2013 by the PCLOB; the Guardian page now shows a later 6 June update timestamp. (3) Apple's newsroom post for iOS 14.5 and Google's Chromium Blog post of 14 January 2020 keep body text in markup the helper cannot extract; they are cited through Apple's developer documentation, the French competition authority and the UK CMA, which quote or date them. (4) Zuboff's definition is quoted via The Observer's review, not from the book itself. (5) Equifax's count changed from ~143 million (company, 7 Sept 2017) to ~147 million (FTC, 2019); both are recorded. (6) 'First public CCPA action' for Sephora rests on law-firm commentary (Arnold & Porter) describing DoorDash as the second.

Known gaps: UK ICO's Clearview fine and its tribunal history; Greece's Clearview fine; the CNIL's €50m Google fine (January 2019; CNIL page removed); the Belgian Market Court's 2025 ruling on the TCF; EU-US DPF challenge (Latombe, General Court) not verified; the NYT's simultaneous Cambridge Analytica report (paywalled, not read); India's DPDP Act 2023 is left to another slice. Web search budget for the session was exhausted part-way, so some leads could not be pursued.

events.title: The Guardian reveals bulk collection of Verizon call records, then PRISM
events.place: The Guardian, Kings Place, London
events.summary: On 5 June 2013 The Guardian published a top-secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order, granted on 25 April, requiring Verizon to hand the NSA call records 'on an ongoing, daily basis', including domestic calls. A second story reported an NSA programme called PRISM, described in a 41-slide training presentation, that collected search history, email content, file transfers and live chats from Google, Facebook, Apple and other US internet companies; the companies denied knowledge of it. The US Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board later dated the first story to 5 June 2013 and described it as the first of a series based on documents disclosed by Edward Snowden.
events.significance: Showed that privacy's walls had moved inside the phone network and the cloud, where people could neither see nor object to collection — the grievance that later drove Schrems, the GDPR's enforcement and demands for user-side controls.

events.place: Hong Kong
events.summary: On 9 June 2013 The Guardian named its source, at his request, as Edward Snowden, a 29-year-old former CIA technical assistant then employed by the contractor Booz Allen Hamilton, who had worked at the NSA for four years through outside contractors. He had flown to Hong Kong on 20 May.
events.significance: Put a human face on the gap between what people had agreed to and what was being done with their data, making surveillance a mass public issue across the democracies.

events.title: EU Court of Justice: search engines must delist on request (Google Spain)
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: In Case C-131/12, brought after Mario Costeja González complained in 2010 to Spain's data protection agency about search results linking to 1998 La Vanguardia pages announcing a real-estate auction, the Grand Chamber held that a search engine operator processes personal data and can be obliged to remove links to lawful third-party pages from results for a person's name. It held that the data subject's rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter override, as a rule, both the operator's economic interest and the public's interest in finding the information, unless the person's role in public life justifies access.
events.significance: Established that an individual can make a claim directly against a global platform about how information on them is surfaced — a person-initiated request with legal force, the first widely used 'right to be forgotten'.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 13 May 2014, Google Spain SL and Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) and Mario Costeja González, Case C-131/12, EU:C:2014:317
sources.quote: As the data subject may, in the light of his fundamental rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter, request that the information in question no longer be made available to the general public by its inclusion in such a list of results, it should be held, as follows in particular from paragraph 81 of the present judgment, that those rights override, as a rule, not only the economic interest of the operator of the search engine but also the interest of the general public in finding that information upon a search relating to the data subject’s name.
sources.note: Paragraph 97. curia.europa.eu's judgment viewer blocks scripted access; the identical official text is served by the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62012CJ0131).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

events.title: Schrems I: the EU Court of Justice strikes down Safe Harbour
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian Facebook user since 2008, complained to the Irish Data Protection Commissioner that, in light of Snowden's 2013 revelations, US law did not protect data transferred there from surveillance. In Case C-362/14 the Grand Chamber declared the Commission's 2000 Safe Harbour decision (2000/520) invalid, holding that laws allowing public authorities generalised access to the content of electronic communications compromise the essence of the right to private life.
events.significance: One individual's complaint dismantled the legal basis for transatlantic data flows, proving that a person could force the system to answer for where their data goes.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 6 October 2015, Maximillian Schrems v Data Protection Commissioner, Case C-362/14, EU:C:2015:650
sources.quote: In particular, legislation permitting the public authorities to have access on a generalised basis to the content of electronic communications must be regarded as compromising the essence of the fundamental right to respect for private life, as guaranteed by Article 7 of the Charter
sources.note: Paragraph 94. Operative part: 'Decision 2000/520 is invalid.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62014CJ0362).

events.title: The GDPR is signed — with a right to object 'by automated means'
events.place: European Parliament, Brussels
events.summary: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation, was signed at Brussels on 27 April 2016 and published in the Official Journal on 4 May 2016, to apply from 25 May 2018. Article 21(5) lets a person exercise the right to object to processing, in the context of information society services, 'by automated means using technical specifications'. Article 25 requires data protection by design and by default, so that by default only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose are processed.
events.significance: Article 21(5) is the first clause in a major privacy law that anticipates a person's software stating their objection for them — the legal hook on which machine-readable signals such as Global Privacy Control and person-proffered terms can hang.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation), Article 21(5)
sources.quote: In the context of the use of information society services, and notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC, the data subject may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications.
sources.note: EUR-Lex (eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj) blocks scripted access; the identical Official Journal text (CELEX 32016R0679) was read from the EU Publications Office repository.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 25(2) — Data protection by design and by default
sources.quote: The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed.

events.title: The European Commission adopts the EU-US Privacy Shield
events.place: European Commission, Berlaymont, Brussels
events.summary: Nine months after Safe Harbour fell, the Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250, finding that the United States ensured an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred to organisations that self-certified under a new EU-US Privacy Shield. The Court of Justice invalidated this decision four years later in Schrems II.
events.significance: A replacement negotiated between governments, not with the people whose data moved — and it did not survive judicial review.

events.title: India's Supreme Court declares privacy a fundamental right
events.place: Supreme Court of India, Tilak Marg, New Delhi
events.summary: In Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, a challenge arising from the Aadhaar biometric identity programme, a nine-judge bench unanimously overruled M P Sharma and, in part, Kharak Singh and held that privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. The lead opinion by Justice D Y Chandrachud recognised informational privacy, warned that threats come from non-state actors as well as the state, and urged the government to put in place a robust data protection regime.
events.significance: Extended constitutional privacy to the world's most populous democracy — and explicitly to threats from private, non-state actors holding data, not only the state.

sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Anr. v Union of India and Ors., Writ Petition (Civil) No 494 of 2012 — Order of the Court
sources.quote: (iii) The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
sources.note: Order of the Court signed by all nine judges, 'New Delhi; AUGUST 24, 2017' (final pages of the 547-page PDF).

sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India — judgment of Dr D Y Chandrachud J (for Khehar CJI, Agrawal, Nazeer JJ and himself)
sources.quote: Informational privacy is a facet of the right to privacy. The dangers to privacy in an age of information can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well.
sources.note: Same judgment also reads: 'We commend to the Union Government the need to examine and put into place a robust regime for data protection.'

sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India — judgment of Dr D Y Chandrachud J
sources.quote: It arises in the context of a constitutional challenge to the Aadhaar project, which aims to build a database of personal identity and biometric information covering every Indian – the world’s largest endeavour of its kind.

events.locationNote: Supreme Court building, New Delhi.

events.title: Equifax discloses a breach eventually counted at 147 million people
events.place: Equifax headquarters, Peachtree Street, Atlanta
events.summary: On 7 September 2017 the credit bureau Equifax announced that criminals had exploited a website application vulnerability between mid-May and July 2017, initially estimating that about 143 million US consumers were affected; names, Social Security numbers, birth dates and addresses were taken. On 22 July 2019 the FTC announced a global settlement with the FTC, the CFPB and 50 US states and territories of at least $575 million and potentially up to $700 million, putting the number affected at approximately 147 million.
events.significance: People whose data was taken had never chosen to deal with Equifax at all — a stark case of data held about people without any relationship or terms of their own.

sources.title: Equifax to Pay $575 Million as Part of Settlement with FTC, CFPB, and States Related to 2017 Data Breach
sources.quote: Equifax Inc. has agreed to pay at least $575 million, and potentially up to $700 million, as part of a global settlement with the Federal Trade Commission, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), and 50 U.S. states and territories, which alleged that the credit reporting company’s failure to take reasonable steps to secure its network led to a data breach in 2017 that affected approximately 147 million people.

Criminals exploited a U.S. website application vulnerability to gain access to certain files. Based on the company's investigation, the unauthorized access occurred from mid-May through July 2017.
sources.note: The initial estimate (143 million) was later revised upward; the FTC settlement uses approximately 147 million.

events.title: Cambridge Analytica: Facebook data of up to 87 million people
events.place: The Observer / The Guardian, Kings Place, London
events.summary: On 17 March 2018 The Observer reported that the political consultancy Cambridge Analytica, which had worked with Donald Trump's election team, had harvested millions of Facebook profiles of US voters to build software to predict and influence voting choices. The data came through a personality-quiz app, 'thisisyourdigitallife', built by the researcher Aleksandr Kogan; about 270,000 people downloaded it, but it also collected information about their friends. On 4 April 2018 Facebook estimated that the information of up to 87 million people, mostly in the US, may have been improperly shared.
events.significance: Showed that one person's 'consent' on a platform could hand over the data of friends who had agreed to nothing — the clearest demonstration that platform-defined consent does not express individual intent.

sources.title: Revealed: 50 million Facebook profiles harvested for Cambridge Analytica in major data breach
sources.quote: The data analytics firm that worked with Donald Trump’s election team and the winning Brexit campaign harvested millions of Facebook profiles of US voters, in one of the tech giant’s biggest ever data breaches, and used them to build a powerful software program to predict and influence choices at the ballot box.
sources.note: The Observer's initial estimate was 50 million profiles; Facebook's later estimate was up to 87 million.

sources.title: An Update on Our Plans to Restrict Data Access on Facebook (Mike Schroepfer)
sources.quote: In total, we believe the Facebook information of up to 87 million people — mostly in the US — may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica.

sources.title: Suspending Cambridge Analytica and SCL Group From Facebook (Paul Grewal)
sources.quote: Approximately 270,000 people downloaded the app. In so doing, they gave their consent for Kogan to access information such as the city they set on their profile, or content they had liked, as well as more limited information about friends who had their privacy settings set to allow it.
sources.note: Company statement, cited for Facebook's own account of the app. Updated 17 March 2018 to say 'The claim that this is a data breach is completely false.'

events.locationNote: The Observer's newsroom at Kings Place, London (shared with The Guardian).

events.title: The GDPR applies — and the consent pop-ups multiply
events.place: Brussels (EU-wide application)
events.summary: From 25 May 2018 the GDPR applied across the EU. Consent had to be as easy to withdraw as to give (Article 7(3)), and the most serious infringements became punishable by fines of up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 83(5)). On the first day, the privacy group noyb filed four complaints against Google (Android), Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram over 'forced consent', as 'consent boxes' popped up across the web.
events.significance: Turned privacy from a promise into a liability on the balance sheet — but its most visible product was the consent banner, in which the site, not the person, sets the terms and the choices.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 83(5) — General conditions for imposing administrative fines
sources.quote: Infringements of the following provisions shall, in accordance with paragraph 2, be subject to administrative fines up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 7(3) — Conditions for consent

The withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal. Prior to giving consent, the data subject shall be informed thereof. It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.

On the first day of GDPR noyb.eu has therefore filed four complaints against Google (Android), Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram over “forced consent”.

events.title: Carpenter v. United States: a warrant for phone location history
events.place: Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Without a warrant, prosecutors had obtained from wireless carriers 12,898 location points cataloguing Timothy Carpenter's movements over 127 days — an average of 101 a day. In a 5–4 opinion by Chief Justice Roberts, the Court held that acquiring cell-site location information (CSLI) was a Fourth Amendment search and that the government must generally obtain a warrant supported by probable cause before acquiring such records.
events.significance: Cracked the US 'third-party doctrine': data a person generates just by carrying a phone, and that a company holds, can still be the person's private sphere.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.title: Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. ___ (2018), No. 16–402, slip opinion
sources.quote: Having found that the acquisition of Carpenter’s CSLI was a search, we also conclude that the Government must generally obtain a warrant supported by probable cause before acquiring such records.
sources.note: Opinion of the Court, Part III-B. 'ROBERTS, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which GINSBURG, BREYER, SOTOMAYOR, and KAGAN, JJ., joined.'

sources.title: Carpenter v. United States, No. 16–402 — Syllabus

events.title: California enacts the Consumer Privacy Act
events.place: California State Capitol, Sacramento
events.summary: Assembly Bill 375, the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, was approved by the Governor and chaptered as Chapter 55, Statutes of 2018, on 28 June 2018. Amended several times, it took effect on 1 January 2020, giving Californians the rights to know about, delete and opt out of the sale of personal information that businesses collect about them.
events.significance: The first broad US consumer-privacy statute; its opt-out right became the legal hook that later made a browser signal (Global Privacy Control) binding.

events.title: Shoshana Zuboff names 'surveillance capitalism'
events.place: PublicAffairs (Hachette Book Group), 1290 Avenue of the Americas, New York
events.summary: PublicAffairs published Shoshana Zuboff's The Age of Surveillance Capitalism on 15 January 2019. Zuboff argued that surveillance capitalism 'unilaterally claims human experience as free raw material for translation into behavioural data', part of which is declared a proprietary 'behavioural surplus' and fabricated into prediction products traded in what she calls 'behavioural futures markets'.
events.significance: Gave the public a name for the business model that consent banners were papering over — and framed privacy as a question of who sets the terms for human experience.

sources.title: ‘The goal is to automate us’: welcome to the age of surveillance capitalism (John Naughton)
sources.quote: “Surveillance capitalism,” she writes, “unilaterally claims human experience as free raw material for translation into behavioural data. Although some of these data are applied to service improvement, the rest are declared as a proprietary behavioural surplus , fed into advanced manufacturing processes known as ‘machine intelligence’, and fabricated into prediction products that anticipate what you will do now, soon, and later. Finally, these prediction products are traded in a new kind of marketplace that I call behavioural futures markets .
sources.note: Quotes the book (UK edition spelling); spaces before punctuation are link/italic boundaries in the page text. The book's own opening 'Definition' page was not read online.

sources.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism: The Fight for a Human Future at the New Frontier of Power — publisher page

events.title: FTC imposes a $5 billion penalty on Facebook
events.place: Federal Trade Commission, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: The FTC announced that Facebook would pay a $5 billion penalty and accept new restrictions and a modified corporate structure to settle charges that it violated a 2012 FTC order by deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their information — including by sharing friends' data with third-party app developers even when those friends had set more restrictive settings. The same day the FTC announced actions against Cambridge Analytica, its former CEO Alexander Nix and the app developer Aleksandr Kogan.
events.significance: The US regulator's largest privacy penalty turned on a simple failure: the company undermined the preferences users had set — the problem that person-set, machine-readable terms are designed to make enforceable.

events.title: Planet49: a pre-ticked box is not consent to cookies
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: In Case C-673/17, brought by the German Federation of Consumer Organisations against Planet49, an online gaming company that had run a promotional lottery, the Grand Chamber held that consent to storing or reading cookies on a user's device under Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive, read with the GDPR, is not validly given by a pre-checked checkbox that the user must deselect to refuse.
events.significance: Defined what the consent banner had to look like — active opt-in — cementing a model in which each site asks and the person answers, one pop-up at a time.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of 1 October 2019, Bundesverband der Verbraucherzentralen und Verbraucherverbände — Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverband eV v Planet49 GmbH, Case C-673/17, EU:C:2019:801
sources.quote: must be interpreted as meaning that the consent referred to in those provisions is not validly constituted if, in the form of cookies, the storage of information or access to information already stored in a website user’s terminal equipment is permitted by way of a pre-checked checkbox which the user must deselect to refuse his or her consent.
sources.note: Operative part, point 1 (interpreting Article 2(f) and 5(3) of Directive 2002/58/EC and Articles 4(11) and 6(1)(a) GDPR). Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62017CJ0673).

events.title: Google promises to end third-party cookies in Chrome 'within two years' — then doesn't
events.place: Google headquarters, Mountain View, California
events.summary: On 14 January 2020 Google announced that it planned to phase out support for third-party cookies in Chrome within two years, replacing them with 'Privacy Sandbox' tools; the UK Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation and accepted binding commitments. After repeated delays, on 22 July 2024 Google said that instead of deprecating third-party cookies it would offer users a choice, and on 22 April 2025 it said it would not roll out a standalone prompt and would not return to removing third-party cookies. The CMA released Google's commitments on 17 October 2025.

events.title: California's CCPA rules make browser 'global privacy controls' a valid opt-out

myths.claim: The GDPR is what requires cookie banners.
myths.correction: The consent requirement for storing or reading cookies comes from Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC), as rewritten by Directive 2009/136/EC, seven years before the GDPR. The GDPR supplies the standard of consent that such requests must meet (Planet49, 2019, read the two together) and mentions cookie identifiers only as an example of online identifiers; it does not prescribe banners. Banners are one — often poor — way sites chose to ask.

myths.claim: The GDPR only applies to companies based in the EU.
myths.correction: Article 3(2) extends the GDPR to controllers and processors outside the Union that offer goods or services to people in the Union or monitor their behaviour there. EU authorities have fined non-EU firms on that basis — for example Italy's €20 million fine on the US company Clearview AI (2022) and the Dutch authority's €30.5 million fine (2024).

myths.correction: No Facebook system was broken into. The data came through a personality-quiz app built by Aleksandr Kogan that about 270,000 people installed and that, under Facebook's platform rules of the time, could also collect information about their friends. The US FTC charged Facebook with deceiving users by sharing friends' data with app developers even when those friends had chosen more restrictive settings, and charged Cambridge Analytica, its CEO and Kogan with using deceptive tactics to harvest the data. The Observer's first report called it a 'data breach'; the harm was a breach of trust and of stated preferences rather than a hack.

myths.claim: PRISM gave the NSA direct, unfettered access to Google's, Facebook's and Apple's servers.
myths.correction: The leaked NSA slide claimed 'collection directly from the servers', and the companies denied giving any such access. The US Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board later described PRISM as a compelled-disclosure programme under Section 702 of FISA: the FBI, on the NSA's behalf, sends selectors such as email addresses to US providers served with a directive, which must hand over communications to or from those selectors. The collection was vast and legally contested, but it ran through the companies under legal compulsion rather than through a back door.

sources.note: Elsewhere in the report: 'In PRISM collection, the government (specifically, the FBI on behalf of the NSA) sends selectors ...'.

myths.claim: Global Privacy Control is just 'Do Not Track' again — a browser flag websites can ignore.
myths.correction: Do Not Track was never made mandatory; the W3C closed its work in January 2019 for lack of deployment and support. GPC differs in having legal force in some places: California's CCPA regulations require covered businesses to treat it as a valid opt-out of sale or sharing, the Attorney General fined Sephora $1.2 million in 2022 partly for ignoring it, and Colorado requires controllers to honour recognised universal opt-out mechanisms from 1 July 2024. Where no such law applies, it remains a request.

signals.name: IAB Europe Transparency & Consent Framework (TC String)
signals.years: 2018–present (v1.1 launched 25 April 2018; v2.0 21 August 2019; v2.1 19 August 2020; v2.2 16 May 2023; v2.3 April 2025)
signals.body: IAB Europe (advertising-industry trade association), with IAB Tech Lab
signals.whoSpeaks: The website's consent management platform (CMP), recording what the person clicked in a pop-up the site designed
signals.whatItSays: Per-purpose and per-vendor consents and legitimate-interest objections, encoded in a 'TC String' that is passed to the companies taking part in real-time bidding
signals.legalForce: None of its own — an industry compliance tool under the GDPR and ePrivacy rules. The Belgian DPA found it non-compliant (2 February 2022, €250,000 fine); the CJEU held the TC String itself is personal data where it can be linked to an identifier (C-604/22, 7 March 2024).
signals.fate: Revised under a Belgian-approved action plan (v2.2, 2023) and again in 2025; still the dominant consent signal in European ad tech. The person answers the site's questions; the person never sets the terms.

signals.name: Global Privacy Control (GPC) — Sec-GPC: 1
signals.years: 2020–present (launched 7 October 2020; W3C First Public Working Draft 21 November 2024)
signals.body: Founded by Ashkan Soltani and Sebastian Zimmeck with publishers, browsers and NGOs; now the W3C Privacy Working Group
signals.whoSpeaks: The person, through a browser or extension setting that sends the signal to every site visited
signals.whatItSays: One thing: do not sell or share my personal information (under the GDPR, a general request to limit sale or sharing)
signals.legalForce: Binding in California as a valid opt-out under the CCPA regulations (2020; now 11 CCR §7025) and in Colorado as a universal opt-out mechanism from 1 July 2024; enforced against Sephora (2022). Elsewhere a request.
signals.fate: In force and spreading across US state laws; still a W3C Working Draft (17 September 2026). A single yes/no bit — it cannot express conditions, durations or other terms.

sources.title: Global Privacy Control — home page
sources.quote: The GPC signal is intended to communicate a Do Not Sell or Share request under the California Consumer Privacy Act, and similar state privacy laws that allow users to opt out of data sales or the use of their data for cross-context targeted advertising.
sources.note: Same page: 'Under the GDPR, the intent of the GPC signal is to convey a general request that data controllers limit the sale or sharing of the user’s personal data to other data controllers ( GDPR Articles 7 & 21 ).'

sources.title: Global Privacy Control (GPC), W3C Working Draft
sources.quote: The Sec-GPC header field is a mechanism for expressing a person's general universal preference for a do-not-sell-or-share interaction in HTTP requests (for any request method).

sources.title: CCPA Regulations, 11 CCR §7025 Opt-out Preference Signals
sources.quote: A business that sells or shares personal information shall process any opt-out preference signal that meets the following requirements as a valid request to opt-out of sale/sharing: (1) The signal shall be in a format commonly used and recognized by businesses. signals.name: Apple App Tracking Transparency (ATT) prompt

signals.whatItSays: Allow or deny this app tracking me across other companies' apps and websites (and access to the advertising identifier)
signals.legalForce: A platform rule enforced through App Store review, not a legal instrument; France's competition authority fined Apple €150 million (31 March 2025) over how it was implemented between April 2021 and July 2023.
signals.fate: Still in place. It showed that a single, system-wide choice is technically easy — and that whoever owns the prompt owns the terms.

signals.name: Colorado universal opt-out mechanism (UOOM)
signals.years: 2021–present (Act signed 7 July 2021; rules filed 15 March 2023; mandatory from 1 July 2024)
signals.body: Colorado General Assembly (SB 21-190) and Colorado Attorney General (rules and list of recognised mechanisms)
signals.whoSpeaks: The person, through any mechanism the Attorney General recognises (Global Privacy Control was the first)
signals.whatItSays: Opt me out of processing of personal data for targeted advertising or the sale of personal data
signals.legalForce: Statutory: controllers must accept opt-outs sent through recognised universal opt-out mechanisms from 1 July 2024.
signals.fate: In force; a model followed by other US state laws. It proves a legislature can make a person-side signal binding — but only for the narrow opt-outs the statute defines.
